children.text: 1297A - Likes Display
Author:
MikeMirzayanov
1297A - Likes Display
There are three different variants to display $$$n$$$: exact number, thousands or millions. Let's find out what range $$$n$$$ should be in for each variant:
if $$$n \in [0, 999]$$$ then we should print its exact value;
if $$$n \in [1000, 999499]$$$ then we should print it as a number of thousands rounded to the nearest value;
otherwise we should print it as a number of millions also rounded to the nearest value.
The last question is how to round to the nearest number of thousands (millions). There are two ways to do it:
we can avoid using numbers with floating points, i.e. use formula $$$\left\lfloor \frac{n + 500}{1000} \right\rfloor$$$ (or $$$\left\lfloor \frac{n + 5 \cdot 10^5}{10^6} \right\rfloor$$$)
or we can use $$$roundToInt()$$$ function on Double value.
1297B - Cartoons
Author:
MikeMirzayanov
1297B - Cartoons

Let's prove the next proposition: if the answer is not equal to $$$-1$$$ then exists such answer $$$x$$$ that either $$$|x - l_i| \le 1$$$ or $$$|x - r_i| \le 1$$$ for some $$$1 \le i \le n$$$. Let we have the answer $$$x$$$ and $$$x \ne l_i$$$ and $$$x \ne r_i$$$. Then let's move $$$x$$$ to the left one by one until we fulfill the condition above — it will surely happens since there is at least one $$$l_i \lt x$$$.

We can use the proposition above in such way: there are only $$$O(n)$$$ candidates for an answer to check: $$$l_i - 1$$$, $$$l_i$$$, $$$l_i + 1$$$, $$$r_i - 1$$$, $$$r_i$$$ and $$$r_i + 1$$$ for all $$$i$$$. And for each candidate, we just calculate the number of segments it is in.
The total complexity is $$$O(\sum\limits_{\text{test cases}}{n^2})$$$.
1297C - Dream Team
Author:
MikeMirzayanov
1297C - Dream Team
It can be proven that there are only two configurations we need to consider:
The subset with the maximum sum, but without the smallest positive element. It's possible if there are at least two positive elements in array $$$a$$$.

The subset with the maximum sum, but with one extra negative element (obviously, it should be one with the lowest absolute value). It's possible if there is at least one negative element in array $$$a$$$.
We can check both configurations separately or simultaneously in linear time and choose the best one.

P.S.: It's not hard to prove that the configuration should have no more than one positive element being absent (since, in the other way, we can return other elements and make the answer better) comparing to the subset with maximal sum. In the same manner, the configuration should have no more than one extra negative element.
1297D - Bonus Distribution
Author:
MikeMirzayanov
1297D - Bonus Distribution
At first, let's reorder array $$$a$$$ in such way that $$$a_i \ge a_{i + 1}$$$. Then the maximum among all $$$a_i + d_i$$$ is just a value $$$a_1 + d_1$$$.

In the first step, let's look at what is the maximum total bonus we can distribute if $$$d_1 = 0$$$ (so the $$$a_1 + d_1$$$ is the minimum possible). We can find the next formula: $$$d_i = a_1 - (i - 1) - a_i$$$ and the maximum possible bonus will be equal to $$$\sum{a_1 - (i - 1) - a_i}$$$.

If $$$k$$$ doesn't exceed the maximal bonus we can distribute if $$$d_1 = 0$$$ then the optimal answer is already found and we can greedily distribute bonus $$$k$$$: give to the first employe $$$0$$$, to the second $$$a_1 - 1 - a_2$$$ if we can (or all we have if we can't) and so on.

Otherwise, we need to increase $$$d_1$$$. But increasing $$$d_1$$$ by $$$1$$$ leads to increasing the maximal bonus by $$$n$$$. So, let's define $$$rem = k - \sum{a_1 - (i - 1) - a_i}$$$, and we can see that all we need to do is just give first $$$rem \mod n$$$ employees additional $$$\frac{rem}{n} + 1$$$ (or $$$d_i = d_i + \frac{rem}{n} + 1$$$) and other employes $$$\frac{rem}{n}$$$ (or $$$d_i = d_i + \frac{rem}{n}$$$).
1297E - Modernization of Treeland
Author:
MikeMirzayanov
1297E - Modernization of Treeland
There are many constructive solutions to this problem. Let's describe one of them — a slightly modified breadth-first search (bfs).

Let's spread our chosen subset from any fixed vertex (vertex $$$1$$$, for simplicity) as bfs does. Suppose we are "standing" in vertex $$$v \ne 1$$$ and have edges $$$(v, to_1), (v, to_2), \dots, (v, to_k)$$$ with vertices $$$to_i$$$ which aren't chosen yet.

We can be sure that $$$v$$$ is a leaf in the currently chosen subset, but what will happen if we'd try to add $$$to_i$$$ in the chosen subset? If we add $$$to_1$$$, then $$$v$$$ stops being a leaf but $$$to_1$$$ becomes, so the total number of leaves doesn't decrease. If we'd add $$$to_2$$$ after that then $$$to_2$$$ also becomes a leaf — the total number of leaves is increased by $$$1$$$.

The starting vertex $$$1$$$ has some extra cases, but, in general, we can see that the total number of leaves stays the same or increases by $$$1$$$ at each step — so we can get any number of leaves from $$$1$$$ to maximum possible — and it's not hard to prove that the maximum possible number of leaves has the whole tree (and it's a finish state of bfs).
As a result, all our modifications of standard bfs algorithm are carrying the current number of leaves and breaking when it becomes equal to $$$k$$$.
1297F - Movie Fan
Author:
MikeMirzayanov
1297F - Movie Fan

The key observation is the following: when we choose which movies to watch, it's optimal to choose ones whose $$$b_i$$$ are minimal possible. It can be proven by contradiction: suppose we have the answer where $$$t_i \gt t_j$$$ but $$$b_i \lt b_j$$$, let's swap $$$t_i$$$ and $$$t_j$$$ and get $$$\max(b_i - t_j, b_j - t_i) \le \max(b_i - t_i, b_j - t_j)$$$ — the contradiction.

Now, let's carefully simulate the process. Let's iterate over day $$$D$$$ and maintain a set of segments $$$[a_i, b_i]$$$ (where $$$a_i \le D$$$) sorted by $$$b_i$$$. The moments of starting airing $$$a_i$$$ will become events.

So we can do the following: for a fixed $$$D$$$, at first, let's add to the set all segments $$$[a_i, b_i]$$$ with $$$a_i = D$$$. Then choose $$$\min(m, \text{set size})$$$ movies we will watch at day $$$D$$$. And finally, if the set is not empty then move from $$$D$$$ to $$$D + 1$$$. Otherwise, let's move $$$D$$$ straight to the next event.

Since there are $$$O(n)$$$ events and $$$O(n)$$$ movies it can be proven that we will check only $$$O(n)$$$ days and there will be $$$O(n)$$$ "first()" and "remove()" queries to the set. So, the total complexity is $$$O(n \log(n))$$$.
1297G - M-numbers
Authors:
MikeMirzayanov
Stepavly
1297G - M-numbers

Note, that since each divisor of $$$m$$$ should be a digit less than $$$10$$$ then all prime divisors of $$$m$$$ should be less than $$$10$$$, i.e. we can represent $$$m$$$ as $$$m = 2^{f_1} \cdot 3^{f_2} \cdot 5^{f_3} \cdot 7^{f_4}$$$. Otherwise, the answer is $$$-1$$$.

Now, let's just write dynamic programming $$$dp$$$ with state $$$(f_1, f_2, f_3, f_4, len)$$$ which is equal to the number of $$$m$$$-numbers of length $$$len$$$ and $$$m = 2^{f_1} \cdot 3^{f_2} \cdot 5^{f_3} \cdot 7^{f_4}$$$. The transisions are quite straightforward: let's choose what the last digit $$$d$$$ is or let's check all posible last digit $$$d \in [1, 9]$$$ recalculate array $$$f$$$ and ask value of state $$$(f_1', f_2', f_3', f_4', len - 1)$$$.
The trick is that we'd visit not so many different states, so it's enough just to memorize all of them by hashing and map structure.

The last question is how to find $$$k$$$-th smallest in lexicographical order. It's quite a standard algorithm. At first, let find the length of the answer. It should be equal to the minimum $$$len$$$ such that the total number of $$$m$$$-numbers of length no more than $$$len$$$ is at least $$$k$$$. Then let's build the answer from the prefix deciding for each position, what digit should be here. It can be done using the $$$dp$$$ to calculate a number of $$$m'$$$-numbers which has a fixed prefix.
1297H - Paint the String
Authors:
MikeMirzayanov
antontrygubO_o
1297H - Paint the String

Suppose (without loss of generality) the first letter $$$s_0$$$ belongs to string $$$r$$$. To find out some properties of the optimal answer, let's look at the following situation: the prefix of length $$$i$$$ of $$$s$$$ belongs to $$$r$$$ (so, $$$b$$$ is empty) and we decide where to put $$$s_i$$$.

If $$$s_i \gt r_0$$$ then it's optimal to add it in $$$r$$$ since $$$\max(r + s_i, "") \lt \max(r, s_i)$$$. If $$$s_i \lt r_0$$$ then it's optimal to add all suffix $$$s_i \dots s_{|s|-1}$$$ in $$$b$$$ since $$$s_i \dots s_{|s|-1} \lt r$$$ and $$$r \lt r + \text{(any letters)}$$$.

The only case is $$$s_i = r_0$$$ and here we should check both variants. But if we add $$$s_i$$$ to $$$b$$$ we can "drop" first letters both in $$$r$$$ and $$$b$$$. So we can see that in any case, the following pattern will hold: $$$s = ps + ss$$$, $$$r \subseteq ps$$$ and $$$b = (\text{prefix of $$$r$$$}) + ss$$$ (of course, $$$r \ge b$$$).

So we can write $$$dp[i][j]$$$, where $$$i$$$ is the length of the prefix $$$ps$$$ and $$$j$$$ is the length the first part of $$$b$$$ which is a prefix of $$$r$$$. The value of $$$dp$$$ is the lexicographically minimum string $$$r$$$ if it exists.

The transitions are natural: for $$$dp[i][j]$$$ we can try to add $$$s_i$$$ either to $$$r$$$ or to $$$b$$$ if possible. The minimal possible $$$r$$$ is either $$$dp[n][j]$$$ for some $$$j$$$ or $$$dp[i][j]$$$ if $$$s_i \lt r_j$$$.
The resulting complexity is $$$O(t \cdot n^3)$$$ but with quite a small constant factor.
1297I - Falling Blocks
Authors:
FieryPhoenix
dragonslayerintraining
1297I - Falling Blocks

If we store, for each height, an ordered set of all blocks currently there then if we know, the height $$$maxH$$$ to start from, we can efficiently enough vaporize blocks or decide that the current block has stopped falling.

We can query the set for that level to check if the fall is stopped (i.e. if the dropped block comes in contact with a block that it does not cover). If so, stop the vaporizing and remember the final height. If not, use the set to determine which blocks to vaporize before repeating the drop.

The question is: how to determine starting height $$$maxH$$$? If blocks wouldn't be vaporized then we could use a standard Segment Tree with "set value on the segment" and "get the maximum on the segment" to set a block on some height and to find the maximum height of blocks on some segment.

In fact, we can use it! It's because of the property that the block vaporizes only blocks it covers, so "setting new block" operation in ST will replace all vaporized blocks with the current one and we don't need to think about methods to erase blocks from ST manually.
The resulting complexity is $$$O(n \log(n))$$$.
